doc.title: Scott Yanow interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 22, 2021

chapter: Daily life and the state of jazz
title: Bulletin board, joke testimonials, and what he is listening to
summary: Chat about his bulletin board and humorous website testimonials, then current listening including Kenton, Anat Cohen and Coltrane.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Listening to classical music, then and now

blocks.x: I like the bulletin board behind you, I wonder what makes your bulletin board?
If there is a colorful picture I happen to get or if it’s something that’s humorous. I’m going after three more but I don’t have the space.

Well speaking of humor, I did a double take on your website when I read some of your testimonials. I said I have to get some of these. For instance Cab Calloway who said “Scott Yanow is hep to the jive.” And you have one from Louis Armstrong next to King Oliver’s, “Scott Yanow is my biggest inspiration of all the cats.”
I want to see if anybody’s paying attention you know. But I mean there’s people there that I never met.
But sometimes you read resumes and there’ll be endless testimonials. Oh this person played at my wedding and you know, that’s all nice but —
Yeah, and the people who include every person they ever backed up, even though they might have been in a 30-piece orchestra, a one time shot, right. “Played on stage with —”
Yeah you have to make it colorful.
What’s on your to-do list at the moment?

I don’t know. I don’t know what I’m doing. I’ve been listening to a lot of re-issues but I mean recently I listened to some Stan Kenton ballad albums because I reviewed it for something, for one magazine. And then a George Duke album that actually has him playing jazz in the early 70s. But as far as new music goes, I don’t know there’s an Anat Cohen record, a Brazilian album, and I’m looking forward to getting the John Coltrane “A Love Supreme” the live version that just came out. But it’s on a moment’s notice. When it doubt I’ll put on Eddie Condon. The thing is sometimes people get depressed and I say, “Well, put on Dixieland, the world’s happiest music, you’ll be happy.”
Yes and I want to take note that you mentioned John Coltrane followed by the phrase, “A Moment’s Notice.” Well done, even if it was an improvisation.

That’s in my mind you know. But I’m constantly jumping between eras you know, what I listen to. You know ever since I first got into jazz fifty years ago I’ve never been bored, except when I’m away from it.
